summary: Declarative relational database engine: describe the desired result set, and let the query optimizer find the optimal physical plan.

rows.code: SELECT col1, col2 FROM table_name
rows.means: retrieves specific columns from a relational table
rows.consequence: Never use SELECT * in production applications; fetching unneeded columns wastes memory, network bandwidth, and prevents index-only scans.

rows.code: WHERE condition (AND, OR, NOT)   -- not HAVING
rows.means: filters physical rows before grouping or aggregation
rows.consequence: A filter on individual rows belongs here rather than in HAVING, because this one runs before grouping and can be answered from an index instead of by reading the whole table.

rows.code: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN on col = col   -- unmatched -> NULL
rows.means: returns matching rows only / returns all left rows plus matched right
rows.consequence: INNER JOIN drops rows with no counterpart; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left and fills the missing right-hand columns with NULL, which is why a left join quietly changes what a later count means.

rows.code: GROUP BY column_name   -- every SELECT column: grouped or aggregated
rows.means: collapses rows sharing the same value into single summary buckets
rows.consequence: Each column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or be wrapped in an aggregate, because anything else would be asking for one value where the group holds many.

rows.code:
HAVING aggregate_condition   -- e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
-- WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY collapses them, HAVING filters groups
rows.means: filters aggregated summary buckets after GROUP BY
rows.consequence: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped; HAVING filters the groups afterwards. Putting a row-level test in the second one works and reads the whole table to do it.

rows.code: ORDER BY col ASC | DESC and LIMIT n OFFSET m
rows.means: sorts result rows and paginates output
rows.consequence: Without ORDER BY, relational row return order is nondeterministic. High OFFSET pagination degrades performance; prefer keyset pagination.

rows.code: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (v1, v2)
rows.means: appends new rows to a table
rows.consequence: Support batch inserts: INSERT INTO table VALUES (...), (...) executes in a single round-trip.

rows.code:
UPDATE table SET col = val WHERE condition
-- run the SELECT form of the WHERE first
rows.means: modifies existing rows matching the filter
rows.consequence: Test the condition as a SELECT before running it as an update. Omitting the clause entirely updates every row in the table, and the statement will not warn you.

rows.code:
DELETE FROM table WHERE condition
TRUNCATE TABLE name   -- whole table, no row-by-row log
rows.means: removes matching rows from a table
rows.consequence: Deletion is logged row by row, so removing everything that way is slow and produces an enormous log; truncation resets the storage instead, and cannot be given a condition.

rows.code:
CREATE TABLE name (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  age INT CHECK (age >= 0)
)
rows.means: defines relational schema, column types, and constraints
rows.consequence: Constraints are enforced by the database whatever the application does, which matters because the application is not the only thing that will ever write to this table.

rows.code: PRIMARY KEY vs FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES
rows.means: unique record identifier / enforces referential relationship between tables
rows.consequence: Foreign keys guarantee data consistency: the database prevents deleting a parent record if child records still reference it.

rows.code: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table (column)
rows.means: builds an ordered lookup structure so a search need not read every row
rows.consequence: Reads that can use the index get dramatically faster; every write has to maintain it, so an index is a standing charge paid on insert, update and delete in exchange for a discount on reads.

rows.code: NULL, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL   -- never col = NULL
rows.means: represents unknown or missing data in three-valued logic
rows.consequence: Comparing anything to NULL yields neither true nor false but unknown, so a row is not matched by col = NULL even when the column is empty. The IS forms exist because equality cannot answer the question.

rows.code: COUNT(*), COUNT(col), SUM(col), AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col)
rows.means: aggregate functions computing values across multiple rows
rows.consequence: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts only the rows where that column has a value, which is the difference people discover when two counts disagree.

rows.code: DISTINCT
rows.means: eliminates duplicate rows from the result set
rows.consequence: Requires the database engine to perform an expensive sort or hash operation across all retrieved rows.

rows.code: LIKE '%pattern%' vs ILIKE 'Pattern%'
rows.means: wildcard pattern matching / case-insensitive matching
rows.consequence: A wildcard at the start means the index cannot be used, because an index is ordered by prefix and there is no prefix to look up — which is when a search quietly becomes a full read of the table.

rows.code:
IN (val1, val2)
NOT IN (subquery)   -- a single NULL empties the result
-- prefer NOT EXISTS
rows.means: checks if value matches any item in a list or subquery
rows.consequence: NOT IN returns nothing at all if the subquery yields a single NULL, because the comparison becomes unknown for every row. The EXISTS form does not have that behaviour.

rows.code: CASE WHEN cond THEN val ELSE default END
rows.means: conditional branching expression inside queries
rows.consequence: Allows dynamic computed columns: CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A' ELSE 'B' END.

rows.code: BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT; / ROLLBACK;
rows.means: groups statements so they take effect together or not at all
rows.consequence: Every statement inside either takes effect together or is undone together, which is what lets two updates that must agree be written as two statements. The guarantees a database makes about that are the reason this is one word rather than a protocol you implement.

rows.code:
EXPLAIN SELECT ...
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...
rows.means: displays the query execution plan and actual execution timings
rows.consequence: Shows the plan the optimiser chose — whether it read the table sequentially or used an index, which join method it picked, and where the time went. It is the only way to see the decision, because you did not make it.

rows.code: COALESCE(val1, val2, ...)
rows.means: returns the first non-null argument in the list
rows.consequence: COALESCE(user.phone, user.email, 'N/A') provides fallbacks for nullable database columns.

rows.code: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)
rows.means: calculates ranking or cumulative metrics across row subsets
rows.consequence: A window function computes a value alongside each row rather than collapsing rows together, so you keep the detail and the ranking in one result.
